purpose: Leucovorin is a form of folic acid (a B vitamin) used to protect healthy cells from the harmful effects of certain chemotherapy drugs like methotrexate. It is also used alongside a chemotherapy drug called fluorouracil (5-FU) to help it work better against cancer. In addition, it can treat a type of anemia caused by low folate levels in the body.
how_it_works: Think of leucovorin as a rescue vitamin. When chemotherapy drugs like methotrexate block your body from using folic acid, leucovorin steps in and provides the folic acid your healthy cells need to survive and function normally. It essentially bypasses the block that the chemotherapy drug creates, protecting your body without reducing the cancer-fighting effects of the treatment.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mouth sores, skin rash or itching, and in rare cases an allergic reaction with symptoms like hives, swelling, or difficulty breathing. Most people tolerate it well.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have ever had an allergic reaction to folic acid or leucovorin. If you are taking methotrexate, it is very important to take leucovorin exactly on schedule — missing doses can be dangerous. Let your healthcare team know about all other medications you take, especially seizure medicines like phenobarbital or phenytoin, as leucovorin can reduce how well they work. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using this medication.
typical_dosing: The dose varies widely depending on why you are taking it. For protecting against methotrexate side effects, it is often given every 6 hours starting about 24 hours after the methotrexate dose, and may be given by mouth, injection, or IV. For use with fluorouracil chemotherapy, it is typically given through an IV in a clinic or hospital. Your doctor or care team will set the exact dose and schedule that is right for your situation.
